• Approximately 90% is bound to CBG.
• 5% is loosely bound to albumin.
• 5–10% is free (unbound) and biologically active.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances. The remainder is free (about 5–10%) or loosely bound to albumin (about 5%).

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Which structural modifications to synthetic glucocorticoids prolong their half-life by more than 50%?
back:
• Halogenation at the 9-position.
• Unsaturation of the delta 1-2 bond (A ring).
• Methylation at the 2 or 16 position.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 723 (Book Page): Halogenation at the 9 position, unsaturation of the Δ1–2 bond of the A ring, and methylation at the 2 or 16 position prolong the half-life by more than 50%.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: How is the degree of lower gastrointestinal irritation from NSAIDs pharmacokinetically related to biliary excretion?
back:
• Irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.
• Most NSAIDs are excreted in bile and reabsorbed.
• Increases local drug exposure in the intestinal tract.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): Nearly all undergo varying degrees of biliary excretion and reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation). In fact, the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: In a patient with renal failure, why can morphine administration lead to unexpected neuroexcitation or prolonged sedation?
back:
• Accumulation of active polar metabolites.
• Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G): Causes neuroexcitation/seizures.
• Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G): Potent analgesic (4-6x parent) causing prolonged sedation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): accumulation of these metabolites may produce unexpected adverse effects in patients with renal failure... M3G-induced CNS excitation (seizures) or enhanced and prolonged opioid action produced by M6G.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: What pharmacokinetic variation explains the risk of fatal respiratory depression in children treated with codeine?
back:
• Genetic polymorphism of CYP2D6 enzyme.
• Ultra-rapid metabolizers show enhanced conversion of codeine to morphine.
• Leads to dangerously high morphine levels at standard doses.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): there have been case reports of an exaggerated response to codeine due to enhanced metabolic conversion to morphine (ie, ultra rapid metabolizers) resulting in respiratory depression and death.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Which urinary marker is used in diagnostic testing to estimate the daily production of cortisol?
back:
• 17-hydroxysteroids.
• Represents approximately one-third of total daily cortisol metabolites.
• Derived from dihydroxy ketone metabolites conjugated in the liver.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): About one-third of the cortisol produced daily is excreted in the urine as dihydroxy ketone metabolites and is measured as 17-hydroxysteroids.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: What are the typical protein-binding characteristics and primary binding site for most non-salicylate NSAIDs?
back:
• Highly protein-bound (approximately 98%).
• Primarily bound to albumin.
• Displacement can cause significant drug-drug interactions.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): Most of the NSAIDs are highly protein-bound (~ 98%), usually to albumin.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Explain the pharmacokinetic rationale for avoiding high-dose meperidine in patients with renal impairment.
back:
• Accumulation of normeperidine (demethylated metabolite).
• Normeperidine has a long half-life and is CNS-excitatory.
• Excessive levels can precipitate grand mal seizures.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): accumulation of a demethylated metabolite of meperidine, normeperidine, may occur in patients with decreased renal function... In high concentrations, normeperidine may cause seizures.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Identify the primary hepatic enzyme responsible for the metabolism of fentanyl by N-dealkylation.
back:
• CYP3A4 isozyme.
• Also present in intestinal mucosa (contributes to first-pass).
• Subject to inhibition/induction by multiple drugs.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): The P450 isozyme CYP3A4 metabolizes fentanyl by N-dealkylation in the liver. CYP3A4 is also present in the mucosa of the small intestine.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: What metabolic feature allows remifentanil to have an extremely short context-sensitive half-life?
back:
• Rapid hydrolysis by plasma and nonspecific tissue esterases.
• Half-life is approximately 3–4 minutes.
• Independent of hepatic or renal clearance mechanisms.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Which morphine metabolite is associated with neuroexcitatory properties rather than analgesia?
back: Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): [morphine] is primarily conjugated to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), a compound with neuroexcitatory properties.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Explain the role of heat-shock proteins (hsp90) in glucocorticoid receptor activation.
back: In the absence of hormone, hsp90 binds receptors in the cytoplasm to stabilize them; ligand binding induces hsp90 dissociation, allowing dimerization and nuclear translocation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): In the absence of the hormonal ligand, glucocorticoid receptors are primarily cytoplasmic, in oligomeric complexes with chaperone heat-shock proteins (hsp).

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Contrast the effect of selective COX-2 inhibitors versus nonselective NSAIDs on platelet function.
back: COX-2 inhibitors do not affect platelet aggregation (which is COX-1 mediated); nonselective NSAIDs inhibit platelets by blocking thromboxane synthesis.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 659 (Book Page): COX-2 inhibitors at usual doses have no impact on platelet aggregation... selective COX-2 inhibitors do not offer the cardioprotective effects of traditional nonselective NSAIDs.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: A patient shows no relief from codeine despite standard dosing. Explain the likely pharmacokinetic cause.
back: Genetic polymorphism (poor metabolizer) of CYP2D6; the enzyme fails to convert codeine to its active analgesic form, morphine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): Codeine... metabolized in the liver by P450 isozyme CYP2D6... poor metabolizers may experience no significant analgesic effect.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Describe the biochemical step inhibited by allopurinol to reduce urate levels in chronic gout.
back: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, preventing the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 676 (Book Page): Allopurinol... reduces total uric acid body burden by inhibiting xanthine oxidase.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Which specific enzyme prevents cortisol from acting as a mineralocorticoid in the kidneys?
back: 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 720 (Book Page): mineralocorticoid effect... avoided... by expression of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2... biotransformation to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone).

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Why must naloxone be monitored closely when treating a long-acting opioid overdose?
back: Naloxone has a very short duration of action (1–2 hours); the patient may relapse into coma as the antagonist is metabolized while the agonist persists.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 581 (Book Page): Naloxone... has a short duration of action (1–2 hours)... patient may recover... only to relapse into coma after 1–2 hours.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: An RA patient on azathioprine develops sudden severe myelosuppression. Which genetic test is indicated?
back: Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity test; deficiency causes toxic accumulation of 6-thioguanine metabolites.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 664 (Book Page): Production of 6-thioguanine is dependent on thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT)... absent TPMT activity... at particularly high risk of myelosuppression.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Explain the pharmacokinetic 'first-pass effect' regarding oral morphine administration.
back: Significant hepatic metabolism before reaching systemic circulation; results in low bioavailability, requiring much higher oral doses than parenteral doses.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine)... may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Which specific drug is a ketone prodrug that must be metabolized to an acidic form to inhibit COX?
back: Nabumetone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): all but one of the NSAIDs are weak organic acids... the exception, nabumetone, is a ketone prodrug that is metabolized to the acidic active drug.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific plasma globulin binds approximately 90% of circulating cortisol under normal physiological conditions?
back: Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG). Also known as transcortin, it is an alpha-2 globulin synthesized by the liver. The remaining cortisol is either free (5-10%) or loosely bound to albumin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why must oral doses of morphine be significantly higher than parenteral doses to achieve equivalent analgesia?
back: Extensive first-pass metabolism. Morphine is well absorbed from the gut but undergoes significant hepatic conjugation before reaching systemic circulation, necessitating higher oral dosages compared to injection.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): ...because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Contrast the chemical classification of most NSAIDs with the specific pharmacokinetic nature of Nabumetone.
back: Most NSAIDs are weak organic acids. In contrast, Nabumetone is a non-acidic ketone prodrug that must be metabolized by the liver into its active acidic drug form.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): All but one of the NSAIDs are weak organic acids as given; the exception, nabumetone, is a ketone prodrug that is metabolized to the acidic active drug.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
coreConcept: Opioid Metabolite Accumulation in Renal Failure
front: Q: Explain the risk of administering morphine or hydromorphone to a patient with significant renal failure.
back: Accumulation of active/toxic metabolites. Morphine-3-glucuronide (neuroexcitatory/seizures) and Morphine-6-glucuronide (potent analgesic/respiratory depression) are renally excreted; failure leads to toxic levels and prolonged opioid effects.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): ...accumulation of these metabolites may produce unexpected adverse effects in patients with renal failure... result in M3G-induced CNS excitation (seizures) or enhanced and prolonged opioid action produced by M6G.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Describe the unique metabolic pathway that results in the extremely short half-life of Remifentanil.
back: Rapid hydrolysis by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases. Unlike most opioids, it does not rely on hepatic metabolism, allowing for ultra-rapid termination of effect (half-life approx. 3-4 minutes).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific P450 isozyme is primarily responsible for the hepatic N-dealkylation of Fentanyl?
back: CYP3A4. This enzyme is also present in the small intestinal mucosa, contributing to the first-pass metabolism of fentanyl when administered orally.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): The P450 isozyme CYP3A4 metabolizes fentanyl by N-dealkylation in the liver. CYP3A4 is also present in the mucosa of the small intestine...

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the protein binding profile of synthetic corticosteroids like Dexamethasone differ from natural cortisol?
back: Dexamethasone is primarily bound to albumin. While natural cortisol has a high affinity for CBG, synthetic analogs like dexamethasone largely bind to albumin, which has higher capacity but lower affinity.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): Synthetic corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are largely bound to albumin rather than CBG.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why does methadone require frequent dosing for analgesia despite having a long elimination half-life?
back: Analgesic duration vs. terminal half-life. While the half-life is 25-52 hours, the analgesic effect typically lasts only 4-8 hours, necessitating q8h dosing for pain management vs. once-daily for withdrawal.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 581 (Book Page): ...use of methadone as an analgesic typically requires administration at intervals of no more than 8 hours. However, given methadone’s highly variable pharmacokinetics and long half-life (25–52 hours)...

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the clinical correlation between NSAID enterohepatic circulation and adverse gastrointestinal effects?
back: Increased lower GI irritation. Nearly all NSAIDs undergo biliary excretion and reabsorption; the degree of lower gastrointestinal tract irritation is directly proportionate to the drug's enterohepatic circulation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): ...nearly all undergo varying degrees of biliary excretion and reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation). In fact, the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: List three clinical conditions that can increase the circulatory half-life of hydrocortisone.
back:
1. Liver disease (decreased metabolism)
2. Hypothyroidism (decreased clearance)
3. High-stress states. Normal half-life is approximately 60-90 minutes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): The half-life of cortisol in the circulation is normally about 60–90 minutes; it may be increased... when stress, hypothyroidism, or liver disease is present.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is the oral dose of morphine significantly higher than the parenteral dose?
back: Morphine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, which significantly reduces its oral bioavailability compared to systemic administration.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 554 (Book Page): [Because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Explain the clinical danger of administering morphine to patients with severe renal impairment.
back: Active metabolites like Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G) and M3G accumulate in renal failure, potentially causing prolonged respiratory depression and neuroexcitatory seizures.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [Accumulation of these metabolites may produce unexpected adverse effects in patients with renal failure... result in M3G-induced CNS excitation (seizures) or enhanced and prolonged opioid action produced by M6G.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does CYP2D6 genetic polymorphism affect the clinical efficacy of codeine?
back: Codeine is a prodrug; 'poor metabolizers' experience no analgesia due to low conversion to morphine, while 'ultra-rapid metabolizers' risk fatal toxicity.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [Codeine... undergo metabolism... by P450 isozyme CYP2D6, resulting in the production of metabolites of greater potency... codeine itself has relatively low affinity for opioid receptors.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific metabolic property allows remifentanil to have an extremely short duration of action?
back: Remifentanil is rapidly hydrolyzed by non-specific blood and tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic half-life independent of hepatic or renal function.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 556 (Book Page): [Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Describe the distribution of circulating cortisol between different plasma proteins under normal conditions.
back:
- 90% bound to Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG/Transcortin).
- 5% loosely bound to albumin.
- 5-10% remains free and biologically active.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): [Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG)... binds about 90% of the circulating hormone... The remainder is free (about 5–10%) or loosely bound to albumin (about 5%).]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which NSAID is unique for being administered as a non-acidic ketone prodrug?
back: Nabumetone. It is a ketone prodrug that is subsequently metabolized in the liver to its active acidic form.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 643 (Book Page): [The exception, nabumetone, is a ketone prodrug that is metabolized to the acidic active drug.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the pharmacokinetic relationship between enterohepatic circulation and NSAID-induced GI toxicity?
back: The severity of lower gastrointestinal tract irritation directly correlates with the extent of biliary excretion and subsequent enterohepatic reabsorption of the drug.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 643 (Book Page): [The degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the kidney prevent cortisol from inappropriately activating mineralocorticoid receptors?
back: The enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts active cortisol into inactive cortisone, which has minimal affinity for renal aldosterone receptors.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 720 (Book Page): [Expression of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, the enzyme responsible for biotransformation to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone), which has minimal action on aldosterone receptors.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Describe the mechanism used to accelerate the elimination of the active metabolite of leflunomide.
back: Cholestyramine is administered to interrupt the enterohepatic recirculation of the active metabolite (A77-1726), enhancing its excretion and increasing total clearance.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 651 (Book Page): [A77-1726... is subject to enterohepatic recirculation. Cholestyramine can enhance leflunomide excretion and increases total clearance by approximately 50%.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which structural modifications extend the half-life of synthetic glucocorticoids compared to natural cortisol?
back:
- Halogenation at the 9-position.
- Unsaturation of the Δ1–2 bond in the A ring.
- Methylation at the 2 or 16 positions.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 723 (Book Page): [Halogenation at the 9 position, unsaturation of the Δ1–2 bond of the A ring, and methylation at the 2 or 16 position prolong the half-life by more than 50%.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which two proteins primarily bind circulating cortisol in human plasma?
back:
• Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG/α2 globulin): Binds ~90%.
• Albumin: Binds ~5% with low affinity.
• Only 5-10% remains free to exert physiologic effects.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances. The remainder is free (about 5–10%) or loosely bound to albumin (about 5).

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific enzyme converts cortisol to its inactive 11-keto derivative in the kidney?
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2.
• Converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone.
• Prevents excessive cortisol activation of renal mineralocorticoid receptors.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 720 (Book Page): 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, the enzyme responsible for biotransformation to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone), which has minimal action on aldosterone receptors.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What pharmacokinetic process correlates with the degree of lower GI irritation caused by NSAIDs?
back:
• Enterohepatic circulation.
• Occurs via biliary excretion and subsequent intestinal reabsorption.
• Most NSAIDs are highly protein-bound (~98%) to albumin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): Nearly all undergo varying degrees of biliary excretion and reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation). In fact, the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does Methotrexate maintain prolonged intracellular action despite a short 6–9 hour serum half-life?
back:
• Intracellular polyglutamation.
• Methotrexate polyglutamates remain sequestered within cells for extended periods.
• This metabolic step occurs in both the parent drug and metabolites.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 665 (Book Page): Both the parent compound and the metabolite are polyglutamated within cells where they stay for prolonged periods. Methotrexate’s serum half-life is usually only 6–9 hours.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is the oral dose of morphine significantly higher than the equivalent parenteral dose?
back:
• Extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism.
• High interpatient variability makes oral dose prediction difficult.
• Only a fraction reaches systemic circulation compared to injection.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 554 (Book Page): Because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which morphine metabolite possesses analgesic potency four to six times that of the parent compound?
back:
• Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G).
• Active metabolite that can accumulate in renal failure.
• In contrast, Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) has neuroexcitatory/seizure-inducing properties.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite with analgesic potency four to six times that of its parent compound.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which agent can be administered to rapidly increase the clearance of Leflunomide's active metabolite?
back:
• Cholestyramine.
• Increases total clearance of A77-1726 by approximately 50%.
• Necessary due to the long 19-day half-life of the metabolite.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 665 (Book Page): Cholestyramine can enhance leflunomide excretion and increases total clearance by approximately 50%.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Deficiency in which enzyme increases risk for life-threatening myelosuppression during Azathioprine therapy?
back:
• Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT).
• Low TPMT leads to excess accumulation of 6-thioguanine/parent drug.
• Affects roughly 0.3% of the population.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 664 (Book Page): Production of 6-thioguanine is dependent on thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT), and patients with low or absent TPMT activity... are at particularly high risk of myelosuppression.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What pharmacokinetic feature allows Remifentanil to have an extremely short, predictable half-life?
back:
• Rapid hydrolysis by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases.
• Independent of hepatic or renal function.
• Results in a context-sensitive half-time of 3–4 minutes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which drug is the only non-acidic NSAID that functions as a ketone prodrug?
back:
• Nabumetone.
• Metabolized in the liver to an active acidic drug.
• Does not undergo enterohepatic circulation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 648 (Book Page): Nabumetone is the only nonacid NSAID in current use; it is given as a ketone prodrug that is metabolized to the acidic active drug.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Why is the oral dose of morphine significantly higher than the parenteral dose?
back:
* Morphine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver.
* This process significantly reduces the systemic bioavailability of the drug when taken orally.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 554 (Book Page): [B]ecause of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Name the two primary metabolites of morphine and their respective clinical effects.
back:
* Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G): Highly active analgesic.
* Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G): Neuroexcitatory metabolite causing CNS excitation/seizures.
* Both accumulate in renal failure.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [A]pproximately 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite with analgesic potency... morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), a compound with neuroexcitatory properties.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: How do CYP2D6 genetic polymorphisms affect the pharmacokinetic response to codeine?
back:
* Poor metabolizers: Experience no significant analgesia.
* Ultra-rapid metabolizers: Risk of exaggerated response and fatal respiratory depression due to rapid morphine conversion.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): Genetic polymorphism of CYP2D6 has been documented... some patients (so-called poor metabolizers) may experience no significant analgesic effect. In contrast, there have been case reports of an exaggerated response to codeine due to enhanced metabolic conversion.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is meperidine contraindicated for long-term use in patients with renal failure?
back:
* Accumulation of its metabolite, normeperidine.
* Normeperidine has a long half-life and is neurotoxic, potentially causing seizures.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [A]ccumulation of a demethylated metabolite of meperidine, normeperidine, may occur in patients with decreased renal function... normeperidine may cause seizures.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: What metabolic characteristic allows for the extremely short duration of action of remifentanil?
back:
* It is rapidly hydrolyzed by common plasma and tissue esterases.
* This results in a very short pharmacokinetic half-life (approx. 5 minutes).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 556 (Book Page): Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the primary protein carrier for cortisol in human plasma?
back:
* Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an alpha-2 globulin from the liver.
* It binds roughly 90% of circulating hormone under normal conditions.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: How does the kidney prevent cortisol from exerting unwanted mineralocorticoid effects?
back:
* Expresses 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2.
* This enzyme converts cortisol to cortisone (11-keto derivative), which is inactive at mineralocorticoid receptors.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 720 (Book Page): [B]iotransformation to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone), which has minimal action on aldosterone receptors... expression of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Contrast the half-life and oral bioavailability of methadone versus morphine.
back:
* Methadone has a significantly longer half-life (25–52 hours).
* Methadone has much higher oral bioavailability than morphine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 567 (Book Page): It is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, and its bioavailability far exceeds that of oral morphine. ... long half-life (25–52 hours).

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Which pharmacokinetic process in NSAIDs is linked to lower gastrointestinal tract irritation?
back:
* Enterohepatic circulation (biliary excretion and reabsorption).
* Greater irritation occurs in drugs with higher levels of this circulation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): [T]he degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: How does the protein binding of synthetic dexamethasone differ from natural cortisol?
back:
* Dexamethasone is largely bound to albumin.
* Unlike cortisol, it has low affinity for corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): Synthetic corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are largely bound to albumin rather than CBG.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What percentage of circulating cortisol is bound to CBG and albumin under normal conditions?
back:
• ~90% is bound to CBG (Corticosteroid-binding globulin).
• ~5% is loosely bound to albumin.
• ~5-10% is free (active).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 704 (Book Page): [Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances. The remainder is free (about 5–10%) or loosely bound to albumin (about 5%)]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific enzyme converts cortisol to cortisone to prevent mineralocorticoid activation in the kidneys?
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2.
• It biotransforms cortisol to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone).
• Cortisone has minimal affinity for aldosterone receptors.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 705 (Book Page): [A mineralocorticoid effect of the higher levels of cortisol is avoided in some tissues (eg, kidney, colon, salivary glands) by expression of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, the enzyme responsible for biotransformation to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone)]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Describe the pharmacokinetic relationship between the synthetic steroids prednisone and prednisolone.
back:
• Prednisone is a prodrug.
• It is rapidly converted to the active metabolite, prednisolone.
• Prednisolone is a short-to-medium acting glucocorticoid.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 709 (Book Page): [In some cases, the agent given is a prodrug; for example, prednisone is rapidly converted to the active product prednisolone in the body.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does CYP2D6 genetic polymorphism impact the analgesic efficacy of oral codeine?
back:
• Codeine is a prodrug demethylated to morphine by CYP2D6.
• 'Poor metabolizers' lack analgesia.
• 'Ultra-rapid metabolizers' risk fatal respiratory depression from excessive morphine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [Codeine... is demethylated to morphine... Genetic polymorphism of CYP2D6 has been documented and linked to the variation in analgesic and adverse responses seen among patients.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why do morphine metabolites present a clinical danger in patients with renal failure?
back:
• Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G) is a potent analgesic metabolite.
• Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) is neuroexcitatory.
• Both accumulate in renal impairment, causing respiratory depression or seizures.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [approximately 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite... accumulation of these metabolites may produce unexpected adverse effects in patients with renal failure]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which opioid is noted for high maximum efficacy but a low oral-to-parenteral potency ratio?
back:
• Morphine.
• It is a strong μ-receptor agonist.
• Low ratio is due to high first-pass hepatic metabolism.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 554 (Book Page): [because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What pharmacokinetic process correlates with the degree of lower gastrointestinal irritation caused by NSAIDs?
back:
• Enterohepatic circulation.
• Most NSAIDs undergo biliary excretion and reabsorption.
• Higher recycled drug volume increases lower GI tract irritation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 643 (Book Page): [the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is initial methadone administration closely monitored despite an 8-hour dosing interval?
back:
• Elimination half-life is long and variable (25–52 hours).
• Significant accumulation occurs with repeated dosing.
• Steady-state peak effects may take 24–48 hours to manifest.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 563 (Book Page): [given methadone’s highly variable pharmacokinetics and long half-life (25–52 hours), initial administration should be closely monitored to avoid potentially harmful adverse effects]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What metabolic pathway ensures the extremely short duration of action for remifentanil?
back:
• Rapid hydrolysis by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases.
• This bypasses hepatic and renal clearance pathways.
• Results in an extremely short pharmacokinetic half-life.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 556 (Book Page): [Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: List three conditions that specifically increase Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) levels.
back:
• 1. Pregnancy.
• 2. Estrogen administration.
• 3. Hyperthyroidism.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 704 (Book Page): [CBG is increased in pregnancy, with estrogen administration, and in hyperthyroidism. It is decreased by hypothyroidism, genetic defects in synthesis, and protein deficiency states.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which plasma protein binds 90% of circulating cortisol under normal physiological conditions?
back: Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG). Albumin has a higher capacity but lower affinity, binding about 5%, while the remainder is free.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does enterohepatic circulation influence the clinical side effects of NSAIDs?
back: The degree of lower gastrointestinal tract irritation is directly correlated with the amount of biliary excretion and reabsorption.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): The degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the pharmacokinetic significance of Nabumetone being a ketone prodrug?
back: It is the only nonacidic NSAID in current use; hepatic metabolism converts it into an active acidic drug.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): The exception, nabumetone, is a ketone prodrug that is metabolized to the acidic active drug.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Distinguish the clinical effects of Morphine's M3G and M6G glucuronide metabolites.
back: M3G: Neuroexcitatory properties. M6G: Highly active analgesic with 4–6 times the potency of parent morphine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite with analgesic potency four to six times that of its parent compound.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which metabolic process allows Remifentanil to have an extremely short context-sensitive half-life?
back: Rapid hydrolysis by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases, bypassing the slower hepatic oxidative pathways.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is meperidine contraindicated for chronic use in patients with renal insufficiency?
back: Accumulation of normeperidine (a demethylated metabolite) occurs due to impaired renal excretion, leading to CNS excitation and seizures.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): Accumulation of a demethylated metabolite of meperidine, normeperidine, may occur... in those receiving multiple high doses... cause seizures.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why do oral doses of morphine require significantly higher quantities than parenteral doses?
back: Morphine undergoes a large first-pass effect in the liver, significantly reducing the fraction of drug reaching systemic circulation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): Because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine)... may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the metabolism of Allopurinol facilitate its once-daily dosing regimen?
back: Xanthine oxidase converts allopurinol to alloxanthine (oxypurinol), a long-acting inhibitor that sustains the urate-lowering effect.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 675 (Book Page): Alloxanthine, retains the capacity to inhibit xanthine oxidase and has a long enough duration of action so that allopurinol is given only once a day.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the renal target of Probenecid for its uricosuric effect?
back: It inhibits active transport sites for urate reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule, increasing urinary uric acid clearance.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 675 (Book Page): Uricosuric drugs... inhibit active transport sites for reabsorption and secretion in the proximal renal tubule so that net reabsorption of uric acid... is decreased.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific molecular halogenation significantly prolongs the half-life of synthetic corticosteroids?
back: Halogenation at the 9-position, typically with fluorine, slows metabolic degradation and increases drug potency.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 723 (Book Page): Halogenation at the 9 position... prolong the half-life by more than 50%.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which plasma protein binds 90% of circulating cortisol under normal physiological conditions?
back:
• Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) / α2 globulin.
• Synthesized by the liver.
• Small amount (~5%) binds to albumin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): 'Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why does remifentanil have an extremely short half-life and rapid duration of action?
back:
• Rapidly hydrolyzed by non-specific tissue and plasma esterases.
• Not dependent on hepatic or renal clearance.
• Half-life is approximately 3-4 minutes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): 'Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Describe the distribution characteristics of highly lipophilic opioids like fentanyl in the body.
back:
• Rapidly localizes in highly perfused tissues (brain, lungs).
• Accumulates significantly in fatty tissue over time.
• Skeletal muscle acts as the main reservoir.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): 'accumulations can be very important, particularly after frequent high-dose administration or continuous infusion of highly lipophilic opioids... eg, fentanyl.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does CYP2D6 genetic polymorphism affect the clinical efficacy of codeine?
back:
• Codeine is a prodrug converted to morphine via CYP2D6.
• Poor metabolizers experience minimal analgesia.
• Ultra-rapid metabolizers risk fatal respiratory depression.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): 'Codeine... undergo metabolism in the liver by P450 isozyme CYP2D6... poor metabolizers may experience no significant analgesic effect.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What makes nabumetone unique compared to other standard NSAIDs regarding its chemical classification?
back:
• Only non-acidic NSAID currently used.
• Administered as a ketone prodrug.
• Metabolized in the liver to active acidic drug.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 648 (Book Page): 'Nabumetone is the only nonacid NSAID in current use; it is given as a ketone prodrug... and resembles naproxen in structure.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Where does the primary metabolism of cortisol occur, and what is its normal half-life?
back:
• Primarily metabolized in the liver.
• Normal circulation half-life is 60–90 minutes.
• 1% excreted unchanged in urine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): 'The half-life of cortisol in the circulation is normally about 60–90 minutes... Most cortisol is metabolized in the liver.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of enterohepatic circulation in NSAID pharmacology?
back:
• Extends duration of drug action.
• Correlates with higher lower gastrointestinal (GI) irritation.
• Observed in drugs like sulindac and flurbiprofen.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): 'degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How is cortisol prevented from activating mineralocorticoid receptors in the kidney?
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol to cortisone.
• Cortisone has minimal affinity for aldosterone receptors.
• Prevents unintended sodium retention/alkalosis.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 720 (Book Page): 'mineralocorticoid effect... is avoided in some tissues... by expression of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2... biotransformation to its 11-keto derivative (cortisone).'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific morphine metabolite accumulates in renal failure to cause neuroexcitatory effects?
back:
• Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G).
• Has neuroexcitatory (seizure-inducing) properties.
• Lacks analgesic activity.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): 'accumulation of... morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), a compound with neuroexcitatory properties... in patients with renal failure.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is the oral dose of morphine significantly higher than the parenteral dose?
back:
• Significant first-pass metabolism in the liver.
• Low and variable oral bioavailability.
• Converted mainly to polar glucuronides (M3G/M6G).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): 'because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.'

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is the oral dose of Morphine significantly higher than the parenteral dose?
back: Due to a significant first-pass effect in the liver, which reduces the bioavailability of the drug compared to parenteral routes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 554 (Book Page): [B]ecause of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which hepatic enzyme is responsible for converting Codeine into its more potent analgesic metabolite, Morphine?
back: CYP2D6 (P450 isozyme) performing O-demethylation of codeine into morphine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): Codeine, oxycodone, and hydrocodone undergo metabolism in the liver by P450 isozyme CYP2D6, resulting in the production of metabolites of greater potency.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Contrast the clinical significance of Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G).
back: M3G is neuroexcitatory (linked to seizures), while M6G is an active metabolite with potent analgesic activity.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [P]rimarily conjugated to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), a compound with neuroexcitatory properties... approximately 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: A patient with renal failure develops seizures while on Meperidine. What pharmacokinetic complication explains this?
back: Accumulation of the demethylated metabolite normeperidine, which is neurotoxic and excreted by the kidneys.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [A]ccumulation of a demethylated metabolite of meperidine, normeperidine, may occur in patients with decreased renal function... In high concentrations, normeperidine may cause seizures.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does protein binding for synthetic corticosteroids like Dexamethasone differ from endogenous Cortisol?
back: Cortisol binds primarily to Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), whereas synthetic steroids are largely bound to albumin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): Synthetic corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are largely bound to albumin rather than CBG.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the typical circulation half-life of Cortisol under normal physiologic conditions?
back: Approximately 60 to 90 minutes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): The half-life of cortisol in the circulation is normally about 60–90 minutes.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific chemical modification in synthetic corticosteroids prolongs their half-life by more than 50%?
back: Halogenation at the 9 position, unsaturation of the Δ1–2 bond, or methylation at the 2 or 16 position.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 723 (Book Page): Halogenation at the 9 position, unsaturation of the Δ1–2 bond of the A ring, and methylation at the 2 or 16 position prolong the half-life by more than 50%.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why does Remifentanil have an extremely short pharmacokinetic half-life compared to other phenylpiperidines?
back: It is rapidly hydrolyzed by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases, bypassing slower hepatic P450 metabolism.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does co-administration of Probenecid affect the CNS uptake of Morphine metabolites?
back: It enhances CNS uptake of M3G and M6G by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein drug transporter.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): CNS uptake of M3G and, to a lesser extent, M6G can be enhanced by co-administration of probenecid or of drugs that inhibit the P-glycoprotein drug transporter.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What metabolic step is required for the corticosteroid Prednisone to become pharmacologically active?
back: Hepatic conversion into its active product, Prednisolone.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 723 (Book Page): [P]rednisone is rapidly converted to the active product prednisolone in the body.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What specific serum protein binds approximately 90% of circulating cortisol under normal physiological conditions?
back: Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an alpha-2 globulin synthesized by the liver.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): [Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the failure of morphine to induce mu-receptor endocytosis contribute to its pathophysiological effects?
back: The lack of receptor endocytosis and subsequent recycling is a critical component in the development of opioid tolerance and physical dependence.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): [the failure of morphine to induce endocytosis of the μ-opioid receptor is an important component of tolerance and dependence.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Contrast the duration of platelet inhibition between aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs based on their binding kinetics.
back: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX for the platelet's lifespan (8–10 days), whereas non-selective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors with shorter durations.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): [Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and blocks platelet COX, while the non-COX-selective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: A patient requires increasingly larger doses of morphine to reproduce an initial analgesic effect. Define this pharmacological phenomenon.
back: Tolerance; a gradual loss in drug effectiveness following repeated administration, requiring dose escalation for the same therapeutic response.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 579 (Book Page): [With frequently repeated therapeutic doses of morphine or its surrogates, there is a gradual loss in effectiveness; this loss of effectiveness is termed tolerance.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the primary metabolic step for the hepatic inactivation of morphine and its congeners?
back: Conversion into polar metabolites, primarily through conjugation with glucuronic acid to form glucuronides.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): [The opioids are converted in large part to polar metabolites (mostly glucuronides), which are then readily excreted by the kidneys.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What cortisol concentration criteria in a dexamethasone suppression test distinguish normal individuals from those with Cushing’s syndrome?
back: Normal: morning cortisol <3 mcg/dL. Cushing’s syndrome: morning cortisol >5 mcg/dL.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 725 (Book Page): [In normal individuals, the morning cortisol concentration is usually <3 mcg/dL, whereas in Cushing’s syndrome the level is usually >5 mcg/dL.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is 'opioid rotation' effective in managing patients who develop tolerance to a specific mu-receptor agonist?
back: Cross-tolerance between different mu-receptor agonists is often incomplete, allowing a new opioid to provide analgesia at a lower equivalent dose.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 579 (Book Page): [the cross-tolerance existing among the μ-receptor agonists can often be partial or incomplete... rotation to a different opioid analgesic... improves analgesia at a reduced overall equivalent dosage.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the 8 am plasma cortisol response to high-dose dexamethasone differentiate Cushing’s disease from ectopic ACTH tumors?
back: Cushing’s disease usually shows a 50% reduction in hormone levels, whereas ectopic ACTH-producing tumors typically show no suppression.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 725 (Book Page): [In patients with Cushing’s disease, the suppressant effect of dexamethasone usually produces a 50% reduction in hormone levels.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which metabolic loop explains why the degree of NSAID-induced lower GI irritation correlates with biliary excretion?
back: Enterohepatic circulation; nearly all NSAIDs undergo varying degrees of biliary excretion followed by reabsorption in the bowel.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): [nearly all undergo varying degrees of biliary excretion and reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation). In fact, the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific hepatic P450 isozyme is primarily responsible for the N-dealkylation of fentanyl?
back: CYP3A4; it is the major enzyme for fentanyl metabolism in both the liver and the small intestine mucosa.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): [The P450 isozyme CYP3A4 metabolizes fentanyl by N-dealkylation in the liver.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific polar metabolites are produced during the hepatic glucuronidation of morphine?
back:
* Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G): Possesses neuroexcitatory properties.
* Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G): An active metabolite with 4-6 times the analgesic potency of morphine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [morphine, which contains free hydroxyl groups, is primarily conjugated to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), a compound with neuroexcitatory properties... approximately 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite with analgesic potency four to six times that of its parent compound.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why is the required oral dose of morphine significantly higher than the parenteral dose?
back:
* Significant hepatic first-pass metabolism reduces oral bioavailability.
* Codeine and oxycodone are more effective orally due to reduced first-pass degradation.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 554 (Book Page): [because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the plasma protein binding of synthetic dexamethasone differ from natural cortisol?
back:
* Cortisol: Binds 90% to Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG).
* Dexamethasone: Primarily bound to albumin rather than CBG.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): [Synthetic corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are largely bound to albumin rather than CBG.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What metabolic complication occurs when high doses of meperidine are administered to patients with renal failure?
back:
* Accumulation of normeperidine (a demethylated metabolite).
* Resultant toxicity can manifest as central nervous system excitation and seizures.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [accumulation of a demethylated metabolite of meperidine, normeperidine, may occur in patients with decreased renal function... may cause seizures.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What unique pharmacokinetic property distinguishes nabumetone from almost all other major NSAIDs?
back:
* It is a non-acidic ketone prodrug.
* Requires hepatic conversion to an acidic active metabolite for efficacy.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): [the exception, nabumetone, is a ketone prodrug that is metabolized to the acidic active drug.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: At what plasma concentration does Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) become saturated by cortisol?
back:
* Saturated at levels exceeding 20–30 mcg/dL.
* This leads to a rapid increase in free, active plasma cortisol levels.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): [When plasma cortisol levels exceed 20–30 mcg/dL, CBG is saturated, and the concentration of free cortisol rises rapidly.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does enterohepatic circulation correlate with the gastrointestinal toxicity of NSAIDs?
back:
* Lower gastrointestinal tract irritation directly correlates with the degree of enterohepatic reabsorption.
* Biliary excretion prolongs drug exposure to the intestinal mucosa.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): [the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the risk of using codeine in patients identified as CYP2D6 'ultra-rapid metabolizers'?
back:
* Rapid metabolic conversion of codeine to high morphine levels.
* Can lead to fatal respiratory depression, especially in pediatric populations.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [case reports of an exaggerated response to codeine due to enhanced metabolic conversion to morphine (ie, ultra rapid metabolizers... resulting in respiratory depression and death.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What metabolic pathway facilitates the extremely short duration of action of remifentanil?
back:
* Rapid hydrolysis by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases.
* Independent of hepatic P450 or renal elimination systems.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 555 (Book Page): [Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short.]

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the characteristic plasma protein binding percentage for the majority of NSAIDs?
back:
* Highly protein-bound, typically approximately 98%.
* Binding occurs primarily to albumin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): [Most of the NSAIDs are highly protein-bound (~ 98%), usually to albumin.]

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: What is the primary biochemical mechanism by which NSAIDs reduce inflammation in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) enzymes. This blocks the conversion of arachidonic acid into proinflammatory prostaglandins.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 643 (Book Page): NSAID anti-inflammatory activity is mediated chiefly through inhibition of prostaglandin biosynthesis... Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and blocks platelet COX, while the non-COX-selective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: How does low-dose Methotrexate exert its anti-inflammatory effect in the management of RA?
back: Inhibits AICAR transformylase, leading to intracellular accumulation of AICAR. This results in the extracellular release of adenosine, a potent anti-inflammatory mediator.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 651 (Book Page): Methotrexate’s principal mechanism of action at the low doses used in the rheumatic diseases probably relates to inhibition of amino-imidazolecarboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and thymidylate synthetase. AICAR... leads to an accumulation of AMP... converted extracellularly to adenosine.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: Which specific molecular pathway is inhibited by corticosteroids to suppress proinflammatory gene expression in RA?
back: The ligand-bound receptor inhibits transcription factors NF-κB and AP-1. This prevents the synthesis of proinflammatory cytokines and growth factors.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): the ligand-bound receptor also forms complexes with and influences the function of other transcription factors, such as AP1 and nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB)... and to a great extent mediate the anti-growth, anti-inflammatory, and immunosuppressive effects of glucocorticoids.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: How does the biologic Abatacept prevent T-cell activation in patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: It contains CTLA-4, which binds to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells. This prevents the costimulatory signal to CD28 on T cells.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 649 (Book Page): Abatacept (which contains the endogenous ligand CTLA-4) binds to CD80 and 86, thereby inhibiting the binding to CD28 and preventing the activation of T cells.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: What is the intracellular signaling target of Tofacitinib in the treatment of RA?
back: Selective inhibition of Janus kinases (primarily JAK1 and JAK3). This interrupts the JAK-STAT pathway, blocking signal transduction for various cytokines.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 656 (Book Page): Tofacitinib is a targeted synthetic small molecule (tsDMARD) that selectively inhibits all members of the Janus kinase (JAK) family... mainly by inhibiting JAK3, and to a lesser extent JAK1, hence interrupting the JAK-STAT signaling pathway.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: Which enzyme is inhibited by the active metabolite of Leflunomide to manage RA symptoms?
back: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase. This decreases ribonucleotide (pyrimidine) synthesis and arrests T-cell proliferation in the G1 phase.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 651 (Book Page): This metabolite inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, leading to a decrease in ribonucleotide synthesis and the arrest of stimulated cells in the G1 phase of cell growth.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: How does Rituximab achieve peripheral B-cell depletion in Rheumatoid Arthritis patients?
back: Targets the CD20 surface antigen on B lymphocytes. Induces cell death via complement-dependent cytotoxicity, cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and apoptosis.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 652 (Book Page): Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody biologic agent that targets CD20 B lymphocytes... Depletion of these cells takes place through cell-mediated and complement-dependent cytotoxicity and stimulation of cell apoptosis.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: What is the pharmacological target of Tocilizumab in the management of RA?
back: Binds to soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptors. This inhibits IL-6-mediated signaling, reducing T-cell activation and acute-phase protein synthesis.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 653 (Book Page): Tocilizumab, a newer biologic humanized antibody, binds to soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptors, and inhibits the IL-6-mediated signaling via these receptors.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: Describe the structural mechanism of action unique to Etanercept compared to monoclonal antibodies.
back: Recombinant fusion protein of two soluble TNF p75 receptors. It acts as a decoy receptor to bind and neutralize TNF-α and lymphotoxin α.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 655 (Book Page): Etanercept is a recombinant fusion protein consisting of two soluble TNF p75 receptor moieties linked to the Fc portion of human IgG1; it binds TNF-α molecules and also inhibits lymphotoxin α.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: How do corticosteroids inhibit the earliest step of the inflammatory eicosanoid cascade?
back: By inhibiting phospholipase A2. This prevents the release of arachidonic acid, the essential precursor for both prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 722 (Book Page): glucocorticoids influence the inflammatory response by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and thus reduce the synthesis of arachidonic acid, the precursor of prostaglandins and leukotrienes.

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which plasma protein binds approximately 90% of circulating cortisol under normal physiological conditions?
back:
- Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG).
- Also known as transcortin.
- Synthesized by the liver.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 718 (Book Page): "Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), an α2 globulin synthesized by the liver, binds about 90% of the circulating hormone under normal circumstances."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: List the clinical states that typically cause an increase in serum Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG).
back:
- Pregnancy.
- Estrogen administration.
- Hyperthyroidism.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): "CBG is increased in pregnancy, with estrogen administration, and in hyperthyroidism."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: How does the protein binding of synthetic corticosteroids like dexamethasone differ from natural cortisol?
back:
- Natural Cortisol: Binds primarily to CBG (transcortin).
- Dexamethasone: Largely bound to albumin.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): "Synthetic corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are largely bound to albumin rather than CBG."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the primary hepatic metabolic pathway for the elimination of cortisol?
back:
- Conjugation with glucuronic acid or sulfate.
- Occurs at C3 and C21 hydroxyl groups.
- Forms water-soluble metabolites for urinary excretion.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 719 (Book Page): "Many cortisol metabolites are conjugated with glucuronic acid or sulfate at the C3 and C21 hydroxyls, respectively, in the liver; they are then excreted in the urine."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Why must the oral dose of morphine be significantly higher than the parenteral dose?
back:
- Significant first-pass effect in the liver.
- Low and variable oral bioavailability.
- Requires titration to achieve therapeutic blood levels.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 568 (Book Page): "However, because of the first-pass effect, the oral dose of the opioid (eg, morphine) to elicit a therapeutic effect may need to be much higher than the parenteral dose."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Identify the neuroexcitatory metabolite of morphine that may accumulate in patients with renal failure.
back:
- Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G).
- Associated with CNS excitation and seizures.
- Lacks analgesic properties.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): "morphine... is primarily conjugated to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), a compound with neuroexcitatory properties."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which morphine metabolite is responsible for enhanced and prolonged analgesia in renal failure patients?
back:
- Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G).
- Analgesic potency is 4-6 times greater than parent drug.
- Accumulates due to impaired renal clearance.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 569 (Book Page): "approximately 10% of morphine is metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), an active metabolite with analgesic potency four to six times that of its parent compound."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of enterohepatic circulation in the pharmacology of NSAIDs?
back:
- Directly correlates with the degree of lower GI tract irritation.
- Prolongs half-life and duration of action (e.g., Sulindac).
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 657 (Book Page): "In fact, the degree of lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract irritation correlates with the amount of enterohepatic circulation."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: Which specific hepatic P450 isozyme is the most important for the metabolic pathway of methadone?
back:
- CYP2B6.
- Also involves CYP3A4.
- Genetic variation leads to highly variable bioavailability.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 570 (Book Page): "The most important hepatic pathway for metabolism [of methadone] is CYP2B6."

category: Describe key pharmacokinetic aspects of major drug groups
front: Q: What is the mean plasma half-life of the active metabolite of Leflunomide (A77-1726)?
back:
- Approximately 19 days.
- Subject to significant enterohepatic recirculation.
- Elimination is enhanced by Cholestyramine.
citation: In book "Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology", Page 651 (Book Page): "Leflunomide... has a mean plasma half-life of 19 days. Its active metabolite, A77-1726... is subject to enterohepatic recirculation."

category: Explain the mechanism of action of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, biologics, and JAK inhibitors in context of Rheumatoid arthritis
front: Q: What is the primary enzymatic target of Sulfasalazine's active moiety in the treatment of RA?
back:
- Sulfapyridine is the active moiety for RA.
- Inhibits release of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, TNF-̑).
- Suppresses T-cell responses and B-cell proliferation.
